en.title: Agricultural Economics: the whole course
en.short: What agricultural economics is, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Agricultural economics applies economic ideas to farming, food and rural resources. It studies how farmers and firms choose what to produce, how to combine land, labour, capital and management, how output and prices are determined, and how policy affects producers, consumers and the environment. It borrows from microeconomics, statistics, accounting and the natural sciences.

The subject has a practical aim: better decisions on farms and in food systems. A farm is treated as a business, but one shaped by weather, biology, seasonality and risk. Agricultural economists also study markets, credit, land tenure, cooperatives, extension and trade. In Nigeria and elsewhere in Africa, agriculture remains important for employment, food and export earnings, although its share of national income falls as economies diversify. The course therefore combines economics with enough crop, animal and soil science to make the economics realistic.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
A first degree is usually a B Agric, BSc Agriculture or BSc Agricultural Economics. In Nigeria, agricultural economics is commonly a department or option within a faculty of agriculture. Programmes often run four to five years depending on the university and entry route, and include practical training. Polytechnics award ND and HND in related fields, and colleges of education award the NCE. In the UK, the subject is often taught within a three-year BSc in agricultural science, agribusiness or economics; in the US, a four-year bachelor’s is common. Master’s degrees usually take one to two years and end with a dissertation.

Length, awards and admission rules differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, universities follow benchmarks set by the National Universities Commission, but details still vary. Always check your own handbook for structure, practical training rules and required courses.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics build the base: the nature and scope of agricultural economics, agriculture in Nigeria and Africa, and the farm as a business. Basic economics, mathematics and statistics come next, because later topics depend on them. Crop production, animal production, soils, fertility and ecology are included so that you understand what happens on the farm.

Core topics apply economics to farm decisions. They include farm management principles, production functions and input response, costs, revenue and supply, farm size and efficiency, risk and uncertainty, and farm planning with capital budgeting. Land economics and tenure, labour and machinery, finance and credit, and farm records and accounts follow. Marketing, price analysis, commodity markets and boards, cooperatives and institutions, policy and planning, project analysis, trade and commodity development, food security, agribusiness and value chains, extension and adoption, natural resource and environmental economics, farm management research and professional ethics round off the core.

Master’s topics deepen the theory and methods: advanced production and farm firm theory, econometrics for agricultural and food data, food policy and agricultural transformation, and frontier topics. A research dissertation is normally required.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study the economics first, then attach it to a real farm or market. For each tool, learn the definition, formula, assumptions and one worked example. Practise with your own numbers: a budget for a poultry unit, a gross margin for a maize plot, a break-even calculation for a sprayer. Check every unit, because hectares, kilograms, bags and litres are easily mixed.

Keep a field notebook. Visit farms, markets and extension offices, and record prices with the date and location. Use official statistics and note definitions. Learn a spreadsheet and one statistical package, such as R, Stata or SPSS. Read policy documents and project reports critically. Work through past questions, and explain each answer aloud; if you cannot explain it simply, you do not yet know it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often mix technical and economic questions. A high yield per hectare is not the same as a high profit, and a large farm is not always more efficient. They forget opportunity cost, treat fixed costs as variable, or compare money values from different years without adjusting for inflation. They use a price without saying where and when it was observed.

Other errors are statistical: confusing correlation with causation, ignoring risk, or generalising from one farm. In policy work, students state a preference as a fact. Name the assumption and the evidence. Finally, check data definitions before comparing countries or years; a rebased index or a new survey can change a figure without any real change.

keyPoints: Agricultural economics applies economic reasoning to farming, food and rural resources.
A farm is a business, but weather, biology and risk make it different from a factory.
Learn each tool with its assumptions and a worked example, and check every unit.
Official data must be dated and defined before you compare countries or years.
High yield is not the same as high profit, and correlation is not causation.
Policy conclusions depend on assumptions; state them and the evidence.

en.title: Nature and Scope of Agricultural Economics
en.short: Defines agricultural economics, the farm problem, agriculture’s special features and the economist’s roles.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Agricultural economics is the branch of applied economics that studies how people use scarce resources to produce, process, market and consume food and fibre. It applies economic tools such as opportunity cost, marginal analysis (comparing extra cost with extra benefit), supply and demand, cost budgets and statistics to choices on farms, in agribusinesses (firms in the food chain), in markets and in rural households. Its scope therefore covers farm production, marketing, agribusiness and rural life. It is not just farming: it includes the whole food chain and the people who depend on it.

sections.heading: The farm problem
sections.text: The farm problem is the tendency, in many countries, for farm incomes to be low and unstable compared with incomes in other sectors. Demand for food rises slowly as incomes rise, while weather and biological cycles make supply change. Many producers are small and cannot set prices. The agricultural economist studies these pressures and tests ways to raise returns, reduce costs and manage risk.

sections.heading: Distinctive features
sections.text: Agriculture has features that shape every decision. Production is biological and seasonal, meaning output and cash flow arrive at particular times. Weather, pests and disease create risk and uncertainty, where outcomes are not fully known. Output is often perishable, so it spoils quickly, and bulky, so storage and transport matter. Land is both an input and an asset. Decisions today affect output months later. These features make simple profit calculations inadequate and call for careful planning.

sections.heading: Roles and case
sections.text: Agricultural economists work as analysts, advisers, managers, researchers and policy advisers. They compare alternatives, prepare budgets, study markets and assess policies. Consider Amina, who runs a small poultry farm near Kaduna. She can sell eggs locally or supply a hotel. An agricultural economist would compare her costs, expected prices, spoilage risk and cash flow, then help her choose a plan that fits her goals and resources.

keyPoints: Agricultural economics applies economic tools to farm production, marketing, agribusiness and rural life.
The farm problem is the tendency for farm incomes to be low and unstable compared with other sectors.
Seasonality, biological cycles, risk, perishability and bulky output are distinctive features of agriculture.
Agricultural economists work as analysts, advisers, managers, researchers and policy advisers.
Good advice compares costs, prices, risk and cash flow, and fits the farmer’s goals and resources.

en.title: Agriculture in the Economy of Nigeria and Africa
en.short: Agriculture’s roles in employment, output, food, exports and revenue, and its changing structure.

sections.heading: Roles in the economy
sections.text: Agriculture is a major employer in most African countries, especially for rural people. It supplies food, raw materials and some exports. In Nigeria, agriculture is important for employment and food output, but oil dominates foreign exchange earnings and is a major source of government revenue (taxes and other income), while services are a larger share of output. In Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Ethiopia and Kenya, crops such as cocoa, coffee and tea are major exports. The shares differ by country and year. Check current official statistics from national statistical offices, FAOSTAT, the World Bank or the African Development Bank.

sections.heading: Farm structure
sections.text: Most farms are smallholdings, often under two hectares, worked by families with hand tools or animal power. They produce most staple food. Large estates and plantations, sometimes owned by companies or the state, grow cash crops such as oil palm, rubber, sugar or tea and may process them. Medium farms and cooperatives sit between. In a village in Oyo State, Nigeria, Ngozi farms two hectares of maize and cassava, sells surplus at a local market, and joins a cooperative to buy fertiliser. A nearby oil palm estate sells to a processor. This mix varies across Africa.

sections.heading: Boards to markets
sections.text: Marketing boards were state agencies that bought export crops at fixed prices and sold them abroad, often taxing farmers through the gap between buying and selling prices. From the 1980s, many African governments liberalised agricultural markets under structural adjustment programmes. Boards were dissolved or reduced, and private traders, cooperatives and processors took over. Liberalised markets mean prices are set by supply and demand, with less state control. They can raise farmer incentives but may bring price instability and weaker support services. Current figures change, so use official statistics.

keyPoints: Agriculture is a major employer and food supplier in most African countries, but its share of output and exports varies by country and year, so check official statistics.
Smallholders, often farming under two hectares, produce most staple food.
Large estates and plantations grow cash crops and may process them.
Marketing boards were state buyers that fixed export crop prices and often taxed farmers through price gaps.
Liberalisation from the 1980s shifted marketing to private traders, cooperatives and processors.
In Nigeria, agriculture matters for jobs and food, but oil dominates foreign exchange and provides much government revenue, while services are a larger share of output.

en.title: The Farm as a Business and the Farming Systems
en.short: This summary covers the farm as production unit and household, farming systems, records, accounts and the planning cycle.

sections.heading: Production unit and household
sections.text: A farm is a production unit: it combines land, labour, capital and management to produce crops or livestock for sale, home use or both. It is also a household. The family lives there, supplies labour, consumes part of the output and shares income and risk. Decisions therefore mix business aims, such as profit, with family needs, such as food and school fees. A smallholder may keep a plot for maize for the household and a plot for cassava for sale. The two roles affect what is recorded and how success is judged.

sections.heading: Classifying farming systems
sections.text: Farming systems are classified by what is produced and how. Crop farming grows plants, such as cereals, roots or vegetables. Livestock farming raises animals. Mixed farming combines crops and livestock, often recycling manure and fodder. Plantation farming grows one crop, usually tree crops such as oil palm, rubber or cocoa, on a large estate with hired labour and processing. Pastoral farming depends mainly on grazing livestock, and may be settled or mobile. These labels are not fixed: a farm can be mixed and partly plantation, and definitions vary by country and textbook.

sections.heading: Records and farm year
sections.text: Farm records are written facts about the farm: plots, inputs, labour, births, deaths, yields and sales. Farm accounts turn these facts into money figures, such as a cash book, an income statement and a balance sheet. The farm year is the period used for planning and accounting. It may follow the crop or livestock cycle, the calendar year or a tax year, so it varies.

sections.heading: Planning cycle
sections.text: The planning cycle is a repeated process: set goals, list resources and limits, compare options, prepare a budget, implement, monitor and review. For example, Amina plans a poultry unit. She records expected feed, chicks and labour costs, compares them with expected egg sales, then reviews actual figures after one cycle and adjusts. Good records make each turn of the cycle more accurate.

keyPoints: A farm is both a production unit and a household, so business and family goals interact.
Farming systems can be classified as crop, livestock, mixed, plantation and pastoral, but labels overlap and vary.
Mixed farming combines crops and livestock; plantation farming usually grows one tree crop on an estate with hired labour.
Farm records are physical facts; farm accounts express them in money.
The farm year is the accounting and planning period and may follow the production cycle, calendar or tax year.
The planning cycle is goals, resource review, options, budget, implementation, monitoring and review.

en.title: Basic Economic Ideas Applied to Agriculture
en.short: Scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, demand, supply, equilibrium and elasticity with farm examples.

sections.heading: Scarcity and choice
sections.text: Land, labour, capital and time are limited. This is scarcity. A farmer with one hectare must choose between maize and beans. The opportunity cost of the maize is the value of the best alternative given up, here the beans income. It is not only money spent; it includes income or food forgone. Because resources are scarce, every farm decision has an opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Demand, supply, equilibrium
sections.text: Demand is the quantity buyers will buy at each price. It usually falls as price rises. Supply is the quantity sellers will offer; it usually rises with price. Equilibrium is the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At a higher price there is surplus, and at a lower price there is shortage. A change in price moves along the curves; weather, income or tastes shift them.

sections.heading: Elasticity and farm prices
sections.text: Elasticity measures responsiveness: percentage change in quantity ÷ percentage change in price. Demand for staple food is usually inelastic, meaning the absolute value is below 1, because food is a necessity with few close substitutes. Farm supply is also inelastic in the short run because crops and livestock take time. Demand for farm products is derived from consumers’ demand for food, and demand for inputs such as fertiliser is derived from the demand for the crop. When supply shifts and demand is inelastic, price swings widely. Example: price rises 10% and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 96 bags. The fall is 4%, so elasticity is −4 ÷ 10 = −0.4. Demand is inelastic.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: These ideas frame later courses. Costs, marketing, policy and risk all rest on scarcity, opportunity cost, demand, supply and elasticity. They help explain why farm incomes are unstable and why policy often targets price and risk.

keyPoints: Scarcity forces choices about land, labour, capital and time.
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up.
Equilibrium price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Elasticity = percentage change in quantity ÷ percentage change in price.
Demand for staple food is usually inelastic, so a small fall in supply can raise price sharply.
Demand for farm inputs is derived from demand for the output.

en.title: Mathematics for Agricultural Economics
en.short: Farm arithmetic, percentages, indices, algebra, graphs and calculus for yields, costs and optimisation.

sections.heading: Farm arithmetic
sections.text:
Yield is output per unit area. If a 0.25 ha plot gives 900 kg of maize, yield = 900 ÷ 0.25 = 3,600 kg/ha, or 3.6 t/ha, since 1 t = 1,000 kg and 1 ha = 10,000 m².

An application rate is an amount per unit area. For 120 kg N/ha on 0.4 ha: 120 × 0.4 = 48 kg N. If the fertiliser is 20% N, product needed = 48 ÷ 0.20 = 240 kg.

A percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Indices follow a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n), and a^0 = 1.

sections.heading: Algebra and graphs
sections.text:
Algebra uses letters for quantities. A linear function has the form y = a + bx, where a is the intercept and b the slope, the change in y per unit change in x. Its graph is a straight line. Solve 1,700 = 500 + 2Q: subtract 500 to get 1,200 = 2Q, so Q = 600.

A quadratic function has a squared term, such as y = 3x². Its graph is a curve. Read graphs by labelling axes, noting units, and checking where the line crosses an axis.

sections.heading: Calculus and optimisation
sections.text:
Calculus measures change. If y = ax^n, then dy/dx = anx^(n−1). The derivative of total cost is marginal cost; the derivative of total product is marginal product. A maximum or minimum occurs where dy/dx = 0. The second derivative decides: negative means a maximum, positive a minimum.

Example: profit π = 12Q − Q². Then dπ/dQ = 12 − 2Q. Set 12 − 2Q = 0, so Q = 6. Second derivative = −2, a maximum. Check: π = 12(6) − 6² = 72 − 36 = 36.

keyPoints: Yield = output ÷ area; convert units before calculating.
Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
Indices: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n), and a^0 = 1.
A linear function y = a + bx has intercept a and slope b.
For y = ax^n, dy/dx = anx^(n−1); set dy/dx = 0 to find a maximum or minimum.
The second derivative is negative at a maximum and positive at a minimum.

en.title: Statistics and Data Handling for Agricultural Economics
en.short: Collecting, tabulating and summarising farm data, averages, spread, index numbers, probability and sampling.

sections.heading: Collecting and tabulating
sections.text: Farm data come from records, measurements and surveys. A survey needs a clear population, a sampling frame (the list you sample from), a tested questionnaire and trained enumerators. Avoid leading questions and non-response bias. Tabulation means coding answers and arranging them in frequency tables or class intervals, so patterns are visible before calculation.

sections.heading: Averages and spread
sections.text:
The mean is the sum divided by the count. The median is the middle value when ordered; the mode is the most frequent. Spread measures variability. Range = highest − lowest. Variance is the average squared deviation; standard deviation (SD) is its square root. Coefficient of variation, CV = (SD ÷ mean) × 100%, compares variability across units.

Example yields in t/ha: 2, 4, 6, 8. Mean = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Deviations: −3, −1, 1, 3; squares: 9, 1, 1, 9. Population variance = 20 ÷ 4 = 5; SD = √5 ≈ 2.24 t/ha; CV = 2.236 ÷ 5 × 100 ≈ 44.7%. For a sample, divide squared deviations by n − 1.

sections.heading: Index numbers and chance
sections.text: An index number compares a value with a base period: price index = (current price ÷ base price) × 100. If the base price is 200 and now 250, the index is 125, a 25% rise. Probability is a number from 0 to 1 for how likely an event is. Elementary sampling uses random selection so every unit has a known chance; stratified sampling divides the population into groups first. Larger, well-drawn samples reduce sampling error.

sections.heading: Reading statistics critically
sections.text: Published agricultural statistics vary by country and year. Check the source, year, unit (kg/ha or t/ha), sample size and definitions. Is yield fresh or dry? Is price nominal or real? Is income gross or net? Is the average a mean or median? Compare like with like, and check the base year of any index. For current figures, use the national statistics office or FAO and state the date.

keyPoints: Mean = sum ÷ count; median is the middle ordered value; mode is the most frequent.
Variance is the average squared deviation; SD = √variance; CV = (SD ÷ mean) × 100%.
For a sample, divide squared deviations by n − 1, not n.
Price index = (current price ÷ base price) × 100.
Probability lies between 0 and 1; random sampling gives every unit a known chance.
Check source, year, country, units, sample size and base year before using published statistics.

en.title: Principles of Crop Production
en.short: Crop production factors, growth stages, land preparation, planting, husbandry, harvest and post-harvest handling.

sections.heading: Factors and calendar
sections.text:
Crop production combines genetic, environmental and management factors. The variety sets potential yield. Climate, soil, water and nutrients form the environment. Management covers land preparation, planting date, seed rate, spacing, fertilizer, labour and pest control. Weeds, insects and diseases reduce yield. The cropping calendar is the timing of operations across the season; yield depends on each stage falling in a favourable period.

Input use is judged by added output against added cost, but agronomy sets the response. Too little fertilizer limits yield; too much can lodge plants or be wasted. Yield per hectare is plants per hectare times yield per plant.

sections.heading: Land preparation and planting
sections.text: Land preparation clears vegetation, loosens soil, controls weeds and shapes a seedbed. Tillage should conserve moisture and reduce erosion; excessive tillage costs money and damages soil structure. Plant clean seed of an adapted variety at the right depth and date. Seed rate and spacing set plant population. Close spacing raises population but may lower yield per plant. Record planting dates; they drive harvest timing and labour demand.

sections.heading: Growth stages and husbandry
sections.text: Most field crops pass through germination and emergence, vegetative growth, flowering, grain or fruit filling, and maturity. Stages differ by crop. Husbandry protects yield: weeding reduces competition, fertilizer supplies nutrients, irrigation relieves water stress, and pest and disease control limits losses. Thinning or gap filling adjusts plant stand. Timing is critical. Stress at flowering often cuts yield more than the same stress during vegetative growth.

sections.heading: Harvest, post-harvest and example
sections.text:
Harvest at maturity, judged by colour, moisture or days after planting. Late harvest can shatter grain or invite pests; early harvest lowers yield and quality. Post-harvest handling includes drying, cleaning, grading, storage and transport. Poor drying and storage cause mould, insects and weight loss.

Example: at 0.75 m by 0.25 m spacing, one plant occupies 0.1875 m². In 10,000 m² (one hectare), population is 10,000 ÷ 0.1875 = 53,333 plants. At 0.15 kg grain per plant, yield is 53,333 × 0.15 = 8,000 kg, or 8 t/ha.

keyPoints: Crop yield depends on genetic potential, environment and management, not on one input alone.
The cropping calendar aligns planting and husbandry with crop growth stages and seasonal rainfall.
Seed rate and spacing determine plant population; yield per hectare = plants per hectare × yield per plant.
Land preparation and timely planting affect establishment, weed control and moisture use.
Husbandry practices protect yield, and stress at flowering is often most damaging.
Harvest at maturity and handle produce carefully; poor drying and storage cause losses.

en.title: Principles of Animal Production
en.short: Farm animal classes, breeds, feeding, reproduction, health, housing and feed conversion for enterprise choice.

sections.heading: Classes and breeds
sections.text: Farm animals are grouped by digestion and purpose. Ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) have a four-chambered stomach and use roughage; monogastrics (pigs, poultry, rabbits) need more concentrates. Purpose classes include dairy, beef, meat, egg, wool and work. A breed is a group with similar inherited traits. Local breeds often tolerate heat and disease; exotic breeds often yield more but need better feed and housing. Breed choice depends on feed, market, climate and management.

sections.heading: Feeding and growth
sections.text: Nutrients are water, energy, protein, minerals and vitamins. Feed is roughage or concentrate. Feed conversion ratio (FCR) = feed eaten ÷ output gained; lower is better. Average daily gain (ADG) = weight gain ÷ days. Output traits: milk yield, eggs, litter size, dressing percentage (carcass ÷ live weight × 100). Example: a pig eats 240 kg feed and gains 80 kg. FCR = 240 ÷ 80 = 3.0. At 10 money units per kg feed, feed cost per kg gain = 3.0 × 10 = 30. A pig with FCR 4.0 costs 40 per kg gain (320 ÷ 80 = 4.0; 4.0 × 10 = 40). Lower FCR saves money.

sections.heading: Reproduction and health
sections.text: Reproduction traits include age at puberty, oestrus (heat), conception rate, gestation length, litter size and hatchability. Fertility affects offspring per year. Health depends on biosecurity (keeping disease out), quarantine, vaccination, parasite control, clean water and feed, and quick isolation. Sick animals grow slowly and convert feed poorly, so prevention protects welfare and profit. Records of births, weights, treatments and deaths help.

sections.heading: Housing and enterprise choice
sections.text: Housing systems are extensive (free range or pasture, low inputs), semi-intensive, or intensive (confined, high inputs, controlled conditions). Examples are deep litter for poultry, pasture for cattle and pens for pigs. Good housing gives space, ventilation, dry bedding, shade, water and waste removal. Management includes feeding schedules, records, culling and marketing. Enterprise choice compares output price, feed cost, FCR, mortality, labour, housing cost and market demand. Housing and welfare rules vary by country; check official guidance.

keyPoints: Ruminants use roughage; monogastrics need more concentrates.
FCR = feed eaten ÷ output gained, and lower FCR means cheaper gain.
ADG = weight gain ÷ days; dressing percentage = carcass weight ÷ live weight × 100.
Reproduction and health traits set the number and survival of offspring.
Housing may be extensive, semi-intensive or intensive, and local rules vary.
Enterprise choice compares output price, feed cost, FCR, mortality and market demand.

en.title: Soils, Fertility and Agricultural Ecology
en.short: Soil properties, fertility and nutrient cycling, manures, fertilisers, soil water, climate, pests and land degradation.

sections.heading: Soil properties and land use
sections.text: Soil texture is the mix of sand, silt and clay. Structure is how particles clump into aggregates. These control drainage, root growth and nutrient holding. Sandy soils drain quickly and hold few nutrients; clay soils hold water and nutrients but can waterlog and compact; loams are usually best for crops. pH, organic matter, depth and slope also matter. Match land use to these properties: do not put shallow or steep land under demanding crops, and improve drainage or add lime where pH is too low.

sections.heading: Fertility and nutrient cycling
sections.text: Soil fertility is the ability to supply nutrients in forms plants can use. Nutrients cycle through organic matter, soil organisms and crops. Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is the soil’s ability to hold positively charged nutrients such as calcium and potassium. Legumes fix nitrogen; leaching, volatilisation and denitrification lose it. Use soil tests and a nutrient budget before buying fertiliser, and rotate crops to recycle nutrients and build organic matter.

sections.heading: Manures, fertilisers and water
sections.text: Manures add organic matter and slow-release nutrients. Mineral fertilisers such as urea, triple superphosphate and muriate of potash give concentrated nutrients. Apply at the right rate, time and placement, and split nitrogen to reduce losses. Example: a soil test recommends 60 kg N per hectare. Urea is 46% N, so urea needed = 60 ÷ 0.46 = 130.4 kg/ha. Water in soil is held between field capacity and wilting point; only the difference is available to roots. Irrigate before stress and avoid overwatering that leaches nutrients.

sections.heading: Ecology, pests and degradation
sections.text: Farming ecology includes climate, pests and land condition. Temperature and rainfall set which crops can grow and when to plant. Pests and diseases reduce yield; integrated pest management combines resistant varieties, rotation, biological control and careful pesticide use. Land degradation includes erosion, salinity, compaction and nutrient depletion. On sloping land use terraces, cover crops and contour farming. Monitor soil and pests, then adjust land use and inputs rather than applying more fertiliser blindly.

keyPoints: Soil texture and structure control water, air and nutrient holding, so match crops to soil and slope.
Soil fertility depends on nutrient supply, CEC and organic matter; test soil before applying fertiliser.
Legumes fix nitrogen, while leaching and volatilisation remove it.
Urea needed = recommended N ÷ fraction of N in the fertiliser; for 60 kg N/ha with 46% urea, use 130.4 kg/ha.
Available water is the difference between field capacity and wilting point.
Use rotations, cover crops, terraces and integrated pest management to limit pests and land degradation.

en.title: Principles of Farm Management
en.short: Planning, implementation and control; factors of production, enterprise and whole-farm budgets, records.

sections.heading: The management process
sections.text: Farm management is the process of organising a farm’s resources to meet the farmer’s goals. It has three linked stages. Planning sets goals, lists resources, compares alternatives and chooses a farm plan. Implementation puts the plan into action: buying inputs, hiring labour, planting and keeping records. Control compares actual results with the plan, finds differences and corrects them. The stages repeat, because a farm is managed in cycles, not once.

sections.heading: Factors of production
sections.text: The factors of production are land, labour, capital and management. Land includes soil and natural resources. Labour is human work, hired or family. Capital is durable inputs such as tools, machinery and livestock, plus working capital for seed and feed. Management is the decision-making factor that combines the others. In the short run, some factors are fixed, usually land and machinery, while others vary, such as seed and casual labour. This distinction shapes budgeting.

sections.heading: Budgets and farm plan
sections.text:
An enterprise budget estimates costs and returns for one activity, such as one hectare of maize. It lists variable costs, fixed costs and expected revenue. Variable costs change with the size of the enterprise; fixed costs, such as rent and depreciation, do not. Gross margin is revenue minus variable costs. A whole-farm budget adds all enterprises and fixed costs to test whether the farm as a whole is profitable and has enough cash. A partial budget tests one change, such as buying a machine or adding an enterprise. A farm plan is the chosen combination of enterprises, resources and practices.

Example: one hectare of maize gives 2,000 kg at 250 currency units per kg, revenue 500,000. Variable costs are seed 40,000, fertiliser 80,000 and labour 60,000, total 180,000. Gross margin is 320,000. If the farm has only this enterprise and fixed costs are 200,000, whole-farm profit is 120,000. Check: 500,000 − 180,000 − 200,000 = 120,000.

sections.heading: Records and control
sections.text: Records are the memory of management. Physical records show yields, stock and input use; financial records show costs, sales and debts. Good records allow the manager to compare actual with budgeted figures, calculate gross margins, prepare the next budget and support loan applications. Without records, control is guesswork.

keyPoints: Farm management has three repeating stages: planning, implementation and control.
The factors of production are land, labour, capital and management.
Gross margin = revenue − variable costs.
Whole-farm profit = total revenue − total variable costs − total fixed costs.
An enterprise budget covers one activity; a whole-farm budget covers all activities together.
Records turn control from guesswork into comparison of actual results with the plan.

en.title: Production Functions and Input Response
en.short: Total, average and marginal product, diminishing returns, production stages, isoquants and profit-maximising input use.

sections.heading: Product and diminishing returns
sections.text:
A production function shows the most output from inputs. With one variable input x and fixed others, total physical product (TPP) is output. Average product APP = TPP ÷ x. Marginal product MPP = ΔTPP ÷ Δx, or dTPP/dx for smooth curves. The law of diminishing returns says that, after some point, adding more of one variable input to fixed inputs raises output by smaller amounts, so MPP falls.

Stage I runs from zero input to APP maximum, where MPP = APP. Stage II runs to TPP maximum, where MPP = 0. Stage III has negative MPP. Rational production is in Stage II; Stage I has unused capacity and Stage III wastes input.

sections.heading: Isoquants and least cost
sections.text: An isoquant shows combinations of two variable inputs giving the same output. Its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution, MRTS = MPPx ÷ MPPy. An isocline joins points of equal MRTS on successive isoquants; the expansion path is the isocline for constant prices. Least cost for a given output occurs where the isoquant touches the lowest isocost line, the line of input combinations with the same total cost: MPPx ÷ MPPy = Px ÷ Py, equivalently MPPx ÷ Px = MPPy ÷ Py. If one input is cheaper per unit of marginal product, substitute toward it until the ratios are equal.

sections.heading: Profit-maximising input
sections.text:
For a variable input, value marginal product VMP = MPP × output price. Under competitive markets, profit is maximised where VMP equals input price w: MPP × P = w.
Example: TPP = 6x² − 0.2x³, so MPP = 12x − 0.6x². APP is greatest at x = 15; MPP = 0 at x = 20, so Stage II is 15 to 20. Let P = 2 and w = 60. Set (12x − 0.6x²) × 2 = 60, so x² − 20x + 50 = 0. The Stage II root is x = 10 + √50 ≈ 17.07. Check: MPP ≈ 30, VMP ≈ 60.

keyPoints: TPP is total output; APP = TPP ÷ x; MPP = ΔTPP ÷ Δx.
Diminishing returns means MPP eventually falls as one variable input rises with others fixed.
Stage I ends where MPP = APP; Stage II ends where MPP = 0; production is rational in Stage II.
An isoquant shows equal-output input combinations; its slope is MRTS = MPPx ÷ MPPy.
Least cost requires MPPx ÷ MPPy = Px ÷ Py, or MPPx ÷ Px = MPPy ÷ Py.
Profit is maximised where VMP = w, that is MPP × P = w.

en.title: Farm Costs, Revenues and Supply Response
en.short: Fixed and variable costs, short-run and long-run cost curves, revenue, and why farm supply response varies.

sections.heading: Cost classifications
sections.text: Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run. Variable costs change with output, such as seed and labour. Total cost is TC = TFC + TVC. Average fixed cost is AFC = TFC ÷ Q, average variable cost is AVC = TVC ÷ Q, and average total cost is ATC = TC ÷ Q. Marginal cost is MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ = ΔTVC ÷ ΔQ. In the long run all inputs can change, so all costs are variable.

sections.heading: Cost curves
sections.text:
In the short run AFC falls as Q rises. AVC and ATC are often U-shaped because of diminishing marginal returns. MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minima. The long-run average cost curve LAC is the envelope of short-run average cost curves and gives the lowest unit cost when all inputs adjust. Economies of scale make LAC fall; diseconomies make it rise.

Example: TFC = 100, TVC = 10Q + Q². At Q = 10, TC = 300, ATC = 30 and MC = 30. At price 40, P = MC gives Q = 15. TR = 600, TC = 475, profit = 125.

sections.heading: Revenue and supply
sections.text: Total revenue is TR = P × Q and marginal revenue is MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ. A price-taking farm maximises profit where MR = MC, so P = MC. The short-run supply curve is MC above minimum AVC; below that shutdown point the farm stops. Long-run supply is MC above minimum LAC; below it the farm exits. Market supply sums individual supplies.

sections.heading: Supply response
sections.text: Supply response is the change in quantity supplied after a price change, measured by elasticity of supply. Annual crops can respond within a season or the next, but land and weather limit speed. Tree crops and livestock respond slowly because of biological lags, gestation and herd rebuilding. Seasonal supply varies with harvest gluts, lean seasons, storage and perishability. Price expectations matter.

keyPoints: TC = TFC + TVC; AFC = TFC ÷ Q, AVC = TVC ÷ Q, ATC = TC ÷ Q and MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ.
In the short run the firm supplies where P = MC above minimum AVC; below that shutdown point it stops.
In the long run the firm supplies where P = MC above minimum LAC; below that it exits.
Profit is maximised where MR = MC, and for a price taker MR = P.
The long-run average cost curve is the envelope of short-run average cost curves and reflects economies and diseconomies of scale.
Supply response is slower for tree crops and livestock than for annual crops, and seasonal gluts and storage make it uneven.

en.title: Farm Size, Scale Economies and Farm Efficiency
en.short: Farm size measures, returns to scale, scale economies, efficiency concepts and DEA/SFA frontier methods.

sections.heading: Farm size measures
sections.text: Farm size can be measured by land area in hectares, output value, capital, labour or livestock units. Land area is common but ignores land quality and intensity. Output or sales measure economic size; capital and labour measure resource size. No single measure is best, and smallholder definitions vary by country, so check the source.

sections.heading: Returns and scale
sections.text: Returns to scale describe what happens when all inputs rise together in the long run. If inputs rise by 10 per cent and output by 12 per cent, scale elasticity is 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2, so returns are increasing. If output rises by 8 per cent, elasticity is 0.8, so returns are decreasing; equal changes give constant returns. Economies of scale are the cost side: average cost falls as output grows, through machinery, bulk buying and management. Diseconomies arise from supervision, labour monitoring, timeliness and waste. Returns to scale are physical; economies of scale are about cost.

sections.heading: Efficiency concepts
sections.text: Technical efficiency is maximum output from given inputs, or minimum inputs for a given output. It is physical and ignores prices. Allocative efficiency uses prices: inputs are combined where each input’s marginal value product, the extra output value from one more unit, equals its price. Economic or cost efficiency combines both: a given output at minimum cost. A farm can be technically efficient but allocatively inefficient, using too much labour when labour is expensive.

sections.heading: Frontier methods
sections.text: Frontier methods compare farms with best observed practice. Data envelopment analysis (DEA) uses linear programming to build a frontier from input and output data. It needs no prices or functional form, but treats all deviation from the frontier as inefficiency, so outliers and measurement error matter. Stochastic frontier analysis (SFA) estimates a parametric frontier with a composed error: random noise plus inefficiency. It separates noise from inefficiency but needs a functional form and distributional assumptions. Both give efficiency scores, usually between 0 and 1.

keyPoints: Farm size can be measured by land, output, capital, labour or livestock units; no single measure is best.
Scale elasticity = percentage change in output ÷ percentage change in all inputs; above 1 is increasing returns, 1 is constant, below 1 is decreasing.
Economies of scale mean falling average cost as output rises; diseconomies mean rising average cost from supervision, timeliness and waste.
Technical efficiency is physical; allocative efficiency uses prices; economic efficiency combines both at minimum cost.
DEA is a nonparametric linear-programming frontier; SFA is a stochastic parametric frontier that separates noise from inefficiency.
Efficiency scores usually lie between 0 and 1, with 1 on the frontier.

en.title: Risk, Uncertainty and Farm Decisions
en.short: Risk versus uncertainty, expected value, payoff and loss tables, dominance, risk attitudes and farm decision tools.

sections.heading: Risk and uncertainty
sections.text:
Risk means outcomes have known or estimable probabilities. Uncertainty means the probabilities are unknown or the outcomes themselves are not listed.

Weather, pests and prices create both. A farmer may know that drought occurs in roughly three years in ten, which is risk. A new pest with no local history is closer to uncertainty. The distinction matters because expected value needs probabilities.

sections.heading: Expected value and tables
sections.text:
Expected value (EV) is the probability-weighted average payoff:
EV = Σ (payoff × probability).
A payoff table lists actions against states. A loss table shows opportunity loss: best payoff in a state minus the action’s payoff.

Example, money units. Good season probability 0.6, poor 0.4.
A: good 100, poor 40. EV = 0.6×100 + 0.4×40 = 76.
B: good 80, poor 70. EV = 0.6×80 + 0.4×70 = 76.
C: good 70, poor 30. EV = 0.6×70 + 0.4×30 = 54.
A dominates C. A and B have equal EV, so dominance cannot choose between them.

For A, expected opportunity loss = 0.6×0 + 0.4×30 = 12.

sections.heading: Risk attitudes and matrix
sections.text:
Dominance is safe only when one action is at least as good in every state. Otherwise the choice depends on attitude.

A risk-averse farmer prefers lower variance at the same EV, so chooses B above. A risk-neutral farmer maximises EV. A risk-seeking farmer may prefer A for its high good-season payoff. A risk matrix plots probability against impact; high probability and high impact risks get attention first.

sections.heading: Partial budgets and trees
sections.text:
A partial budget assesses a small change. It adds added returns and reduced costs, then subtracts added costs and reduced returns. If a spray costs 20 and expected added revenue is 50, the net gain is 50 − 20 = 30.

A decision tree shows choices and chance events. Square nodes are decisions, circle nodes are chances. Roll back by multiplying each branch payoff by its probability and adding at each chance node. Use the result with the farmer’s risk attitude.

keyPoints: Risk has estimable probabilities; uncertainty does not.
Expected value is EV = Σ (payoff × probability).
An action is dominated if another is at least as good in every state and better in one.
A risk-averse farmer prefers lower variance at the same expected value.
A partial budget compares added returns and reduced costs with added costs and reduced returns.
A decision tree rolls back expected values from chance nodes to decision nodes.

en.title: Farm Planning and Capital Budgeting
en.short: Gross margin analysis, linear programming for farm plans, and NPV, IRR and payback appraisal.

sections.heading: Gross margin analysis
sections.text: A gross margin is an enterprise’s gross output minus its variable costs. It leaves out fixed costs, so it compares enterprises only when those fixed costs would be unchanged. For example, maize on one hectare gives output worth 180,000 and variable costs of 110,000, so its gross margin is 70,000. Beans give 95,000 minus 60,000, a gross margin of 35,000. Maize looks better per hectare, but land, labour and cash limits may change the best plan.

sections.heading: Linear programming
sections.text: Linear programming chooses enterprise levels to maximise total gross margin under constraints. Let x and y be hectares of maize and beans. Maximise 70,000x + 35,000y subject to x + y ≤ 10 (land), 15x + 10y ≤ 120 (labour days), x, y ≥ 0. The best corner is x = 8, y = 0: gross margin = 560,000. It uses 8 of the 10 hectares and all 120 labour days. Check: the corner x = 4, y = 6 gives only 490,000; all beans gives 350,000; all maize needs 150 labour days and is infeasible.

sections.heading: Investment appraisal
sections.text: Capital budgeting, or investment appraisal, compares projects whose cash flows come at different times. Money received later is worth less, so future cash flows are discounted at rate r. Net present value (NPV) is the present value of inflows minus the initial outlay: NPV = Σ CFt ÷ (1 + r)^t − C0. Accept a project if NPV is positive. The internal rate of return (IRR) is the r that makes NPV zero; compare it with the cost of capital. Payback is the time to recover the outlay. It is simple but ignores the time value of money and later cash flows.

keyPoints: Gross margin = gross output − variable costs; use it to compare enterprises when fixed costs do not change.
Linear programming maximises total gross margin subject to resource constraints: maximise Σ gmj xj subject to Σ aij xj ≤ bi and xj ≥ 0.
NPV = Σ CFt ÷ (1 + r)^t − C0; accept a project when NPV is positive.
IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero; compare it with the cost of capital.
Payback is the time to recover the initial outlay; it ignores the time value of money and cash flows after payback.
In the example, 8 hectares of maize and no beans give the highest feasible gross margin, 560,000.

en.title: Agricultural Land Economics and Land Tenure
en.short: Land as a factor, rent theories, tenure systems, reform, titling and land administration.

sections.heading: Land as a factor
sections.text:
Land means the natural resources used in production: soil, water, minerals and climate. As a factor it is fixed in supply, immobile and heterogeneous. Quality and location differ, so returns differ.

Because supply is fixed, extra labour and capital on a given plot eventually meet diminishing returns. Land use depends on soil and climate, location and market access, infrastructure, tenure security and policy. Land economics asks how these factors guide land to profitable use without destroying it.

sections.heading: Rent theories
sections.text:
Economic rent is payment to a factor above its transfer earnings, the amount needed to keep it in its present use. Ricardian rent arises from differences in fertility and location: marginal land earns no rent, better land earns differential rent. Neoclassical economics treats rent as a surplus over opportunity cost. Bid-rent theory says users compete for sites near markets or roads, and the highest bid sets the use.

Example: two equal plots, one near a market. If the near plot earns 200,000 naira more profit a year, a tenant could pay up to 200,000 naira extra rent. Check: 200,000 − 0 = 200,000.

sections.heading: Tenure, reform and titling
sections.text:
Land tenure is the set of rules saying who may use land, for how long and on what conditions. Customary tenure holds land under community or family authority, often orally, with use rights rather than sale rights. Leasehold gives use for a fixed term, usually for rent. Freehold gives indefinite ownership, subject to state powers such as compulsory acquisition and taxation. In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in each state governor, who holds it in trust. The governor grants statutory rights of occupancy, and local governments grant customary rights of occupancy.

Land reform includes redistribution, consolidation and titling. Registration records rights; titling gives legal title. Titling can improve credit access and reduce disputes, but may favour elites or men and ignore secondary rights. Land administration covers records, valuation, taxation and disputes. Rules differ by country, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: Land is fixed in supply, immobile and heterogeneous, so its return depends on quality and location.
Economic rent = payment − transfer earnings; Ricardian rent is differential rent from fertility and location.
Bid-rent theory explains land use by competition for accessible sites.
Customary tenure is community or family based; leasehold is time limited; freehold is indefinite but subject to state powers.
In Nigeria the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in state governors and provides rights of occupancy; other African countries have their own laws.
Titling can improve credit and reduce disputes but may exclude women, migrants or secondary rights holders.

en.title: Farm Labour and Machinery Economics
en.short: Labour supply, peak seasons, labour efficiency and cost, field capacity, machinery costs and ownership choices.

sections.heading: Labour supply and peaks
sections.text: Farm labour demand is seasonal. Family labour is the operator and household; it is flexible but limited by health, school and other work. Permanent hired labour works all year. Casual labour is hired by day or task for weeding, planting and harvest. Peak demand comes from tasks that must be done in a short weather window. Missed peaks cut yield and quality. Supply depends on wages, migration, off-farm jobs and local labour law, which differs by country.

sections.heading: Labour efficiency and cost
sections.text:
Labour efficiency compares work done with labour used. Use hours per hectare and output per labour hour (output ÷ hours). Labour cost per hectare = total labour cost ÷ hectares.

Example: 4 workers weed 3 ha in 6 days of 8 hours at 1,500 per worker-day. Worker-days = 4 × 6 = 24. Hours = 24 × 8 = 192. Hours per hectare = 192 ÷ 3 = 64. Cost = 24 × 1,500 = 36,000. Cost per hectare = 36,000 ÷ 3 = 12,000. If output is 9 tonnes, output per labour hour = 9,000 kg ÷ 192 h = 46.9 kg/h.

sections.heading: Field capacity
sections.text:
Field capacity is area covered per hour. Theoretical field capacity (ha/h) = working width (m) × speed (km/h) ÷ 10. Effective field capacity = theoretical × field efficiency, allowing for turns and stops.

Example: 3 m at 6 km/h gives 3 × 6 ÷ 10 = 1.8 ha/h. At 80% efficiency, effective capacity is 1.44 ha/h; 10 ha takes 10 ÷ 1.44 = 6.94 h.

sections.heading: Machinery costs and choice
sections.text: Machinery costs are fixed and variable. Fixed costs include depreciation, interest, insurance and shelter; they arise whether the machine works or not. Variable costs include fuel, repairs, maintenance and labour. Compare owned, hired and contractor options on total cost for the work needed, including timeliness and risk. Ownership suits high annual use; hiring or contractors suit low use. Depreciation methods and tax rules vary by country, so check local guidance.

keyPoints: Peak labour demand is driven by short weather windows.
Labour efficiency can be measured as hours per hectare and output per labour hour.
Labour cost per hectare = total labour cost ÷ hectares.
Theoretical field capacity (ha/h) = width (m) × speed (km/h) ÷ 10.
Effective field capacity = theoretical capacity × field efficiency.
Owned machinery suits high annual use; hired or contractor machinery suits low use.

en.title: Agricultural Finance and Credit
en.short: Farm finance versus credit, lenders and terms, appraisal, collateral, interest and repayment.

sections.heading: Finance and credit
sections.text:
Farm finance is the management of all money on the farm: cash flow, budgets, investment choices and sources of funds such as the farmer’s own savings, retained profit, grants and loans. Agricultural credit is narrower: money or inputs lent to a farmer that must be repaid, usually with interest.

Credit is one source of farm finance. Finance asks whether an investment pays; credit asks whether the farmer can borrow, on what terms, and repay on time.

sections.heading: Sources and terms
sections.text:
Commercial banks give larger loans and overdrafts, but usually demand collateral, records and a business plan. Microfinance institutions lend small amounts, often through group liability and frequent instalments, at higher effective interest. Cooperatives pool members’ savings and lend at modest cost, though funds are limited.

Government schemes may subsidise interest, guarantee part of a loan or target farmers; terms vary by country and change, so check current official sources. Key terms are principal, interest rate, tenor (the loan’s duration), grace period, collateral and repayment schedule.

sections.heading: Appraisal and collateral
sections.text:
Loan appraisal checks technical feasibility, market prospects, the farmer’s management and records, and above all repayment capacity from expected cash flow. Collateral is an asset pledged as security; if repayment fails, the lender may sell it. Common forms are land, buildings, equipment, livestock, savings or a guarantor. Land title is often weak under customary tenure, so lenders use group liability or warehouse receipts, where a stored crop serves as security.

Repayment may be equal instalments, seasonal after harvest, or one bullet payment (a single lump sum at the end). A grace period, a pause before repayments begin, helps investments that earn income later.

sections.heading: Interest and lending problems
sections.text:
Simple interest = principal × rate × time. A loan of 200,000 at 12% for 9 months costs 200,000 × 0.12 × 9/12 = 18,000. For equal monthly repayment, use payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where r is the monthly rate and n the number of payments.

Lending to farmers is risky because yields, prices and rainfall vary, collateral is weak, records are poor, loans are small and seasonal, and delays between planting and harvest strain repayment.

keyPoints: Farm finance covers all money management; agricultural credit is borrowed money or inputs repaid with interest.
Commercial banks, microfinance institutions, cooperatives and government schemes differ in loan size, cost, collateral and terms.
Loan appraisal centres on repayment capacity from expected cash flow, not only on the project idea.
Collateral is pledged security; weak land title can be replaced by group liability, guarantors or warehouse receipts.
Simple interest = principal × rate × time; equal repayment uses payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n).
Lending to farmers is risky because yields, prices and rainfall vary and repayment is seasonal.

en.title: Farm Business Management, Records and Accounts
en.short: Farm cash books, inventories, profit and loss, balance sheets, income measures and financial ratios.

sections.heading: Records and cash book
sections.text: Farm records are written facts about money, production and assets. The cash book records cash received and paid, often with bank columns. It shows cash position but not profit, because it ignores unpaid bills, inventory changes and depreciation. An inventory lists assets and produce with quantities and values at a date. Regular records support planning, credit applications, tax, and comparison of actual results with budgets.

sections.heading: Profit and loss account
sections.text: The profit and loss account, or income statement, matches farm revenue with expenses for a period. Revenue includes sales, home use and inventory gains. Expenses include seed, feed, fuel, wages, repairs, depreciation and interest. Depreciation spreads the cost of a durable asset over its useful life. The balance sheet is a snapshot at a date: assets minus liabilities equal net worth. It shows solvency and liquidity, not profit.

sections.heading: Income measures
sections.text:
Gross farm income (GFI) is the value of farm production. A common formula is cash sales + home consumption + closing inventory − opening inventory. Net farm income (NFI) = GFI − cash operating expenses − depreciation − paid interest. Family labour income = NFI + value of unpaid family labour. Conventions vary, so state yours.

Example: sales 100,000, home use 5,000, inventory rise 10,000, so GFI = 115,000. Operating expenses 45,000, depreciation 10,000, interest 5,000. NFI = 55,000. Unpaid family labour 20,000 gives family labour income 75,000.

sections.heading: Returns and ratios
sections.text: Return on assets = (NFI + paid interest) ÷ average total assets. With average assets 300,000, it is (55,000 + 5,000) ÷ 300,000 = 20%. Return on equity = NFI ÷ average net worth. With average net worth 200,000, it is 55,000 ÷ 200,000 = 27.5%. The current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities, here 60,000 ÷ 30,000 = 2.0. Debt-to-asset = total liabilities ÷ total assets = 100,000 ÷ 300,000 = 0.33. The operating expense ratio = operating expenses ÷ GFI = 45,000 ÷ 115,000 = 39.1%. Use ratios with records to spot problems, compare years and support loan decisions.

keyPoints: Cash books record cash flow; inventories value assets and produce at a date.
The profit and loss account measures profit over a period; the balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and net worth at a date.
Gross farm income = cash sales + home consumption + closing inventory − opening inventory, but state the convention used.
Net farm income = gross farm income − cash operating expenses − depreciation − paid interest; family labour income = net farm income + unpaid family labour.
Return on assets = (net farm income + paid interest) ÷ average total assets; return on equity = net farm income ÷ average net worth.
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; debt-to-asset = total liabilities ÷ total assets; use records and ratios to plan, monitor and borrow.

en.title: Principles of Agricultural Marketing
en.short: Marketing functions, middlemen, margins, price spreads, market structure and channel efficiency.

sections.heading: Functions and middlemen
sections.text:
Marketing moves food from farm to consumer. Exchange functions are buying and selling. Physical functions are transport, storage and processing. Facilitating functions include grading, financing, risk bearing and market information. Transport creates place utility, storage creates time utility, and processing creates form utility. Grading sorts produce into uniform lots, reducing uncertainty and helping buyers compare prices.

Middlemen perform these functions. Assemblers gather small lots from many farms; wholesalers buy in bulk and resell; retailers sell to final consumers; brokers and agents negotiate without owning goods; processors transform raw produce. They earn margins for service and risk. They are not automatically wasteful: bypassing them can raise the farmer’s costs.

sections.heading: Margins and spreads
sections.text:
The marketing margin, or farm-retail price spread, is the consumer price minus the producer price for the same quantity. It covers marketing costs plus the profits of the firms involved. A gross margin is the spread before costs are deducted; a net margin subtracts them to show profit.

Example: a 50 kg bag sells to consumers at ₦1,200 and the farmer receives ₦800. Gross margin = 1,200 − 800 = ₦400. Transport ₦150, storage ₦50, grading and handling ₦50, and financing ₦30 total ₦280. Net margin = 400 − 280 = ₦120. Producer share = 800 ÷ 1,200 = 66.7 per cent. Margins differ by commodity, place and season, so compare like with like.

sections.heading: Structure, conduct, efficiency
sections.text:
Market structure describes the number and size of buyers and sellers, product differences, entry barriers and information. Conduct is how firms behave: pricing, contracting, advertising and collusion. Structure and conduct affect performance, including marketing costs and how prices reach farmers.

An efficient food channel delivers the product consumers want at least cost, with prices that reflect scarcity and quality. Efficiency is not the same as a small margin: a high margin may pay for needed storage or transport. Look for avoidable losses, weak competition, poor information and excessive handling. Many smallholders face high transaction costs, so groups, contracts and better information can improve their bargaining position.

keyPoints: Marketing functions are exchange (buying, selling), physical (transport, storage, processing) and facilitating (grading, financing, risk bearing, information).
Middlemen such as assemblers, wholesalers, retailers, brokers and processors perform these functions and earn margins.
Marketing margin or price spread = consumer price − producer price for the same quantity.
Net margin = gross margin − marketing costs; producer share = producer price ÷ consumer price × 100.
Market structure covers buyers, sellers, entry barriers and information; conduct covers pricing and other behaviour.
Efficiency means delivering the product at least cost with prices that reflect scarcity and quality; a large margin is not proof of inefficiency.

en.title: Agricultural Price Analysis and Forecasting
en.short: Farm price formation, price series, seasonal and cyclical patterns, indices, forecasting and the cobweb model.

sections.heading: Prices along the chain
sections.text:
Farm prices are set by demand and supply, but demand for a farm product is derived demand: it comes from consumers’ demand for food and fibre. Supply is inelastic in the short run because crops and livestock need time.

Along the marketing chain, the farm-gate price is what the farmer receives; wholesale and retail prices add handling, transport, storage and margins. The marketing margin is retail price minus farm-gate price. It covers costs and profit, and can widen with market power or waste.

sections.heading: Price series and forecasting
sections.text:
A price series is a set of prices ordered through time. Analysts separate trend, seasonal and cyclical movements. A seasonal pattern repeats within the year; a cycle lasts several years. A seasonal index is (average price in that month ÷ overall average price) × 100. A price index is (current price ÷ base-period price) × 100. Deflate nominal prices by a general price index: real price = nominal price ÷ price index × 100.

Forecasting uses judgement and time-series or causal models. Moving averages smooth noise; trend lines and seasonal adjustment project patterns; ARIMA models use past values and errors. Test forecasts with error measures such as MAE or RMSE.

sections.heading: Cobweb model and example
sections.text:
The cobweb model explains cycles when supply responds to last year’s price: Qs_t = a + bP_{t−1}; Qd_t = c − dP_t. Equilibrium is P* = (c − a) ÷ (b + d). If b ÷ d > 1, cycles widen; if < 1, they shrink.

Take Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 20 + 3P_{t−1}. Equilibrium: 100 − 2P = 20 + 3P, so P* = 16. Start at P0 = 10. Then Qs1 = 50, so P1 = 25. Next Qs2 = 95, so P2 = 2.5. Then Qs3 = 27.5, so P3 = 36.25. Since b ÷ d = 1.5 > 1, the cycle widens.

keyPoints: Farm-gate price is set by demand and supply, but farm demand is derived from final food demand and short-run supply is inelastic.
The marketing margin is retail price minus farm-gate price and covers handling, transport, storage, costs and profit.
A price series separates trend, seasonal and cyclical movements; a seasonal index is (month average ÷ overall average) × 100.
A price index is (current price ÷ base-period price) × 100, and real price = nominal price ÷ price index × 100.
Forecasting can use moving averages, trend and seasonal models, or ARIMA, checked with MAE or RMSE.
In the cobweb model, Qs_t = a + bP_{t−1} and Qd_t = c − dP_t, with P* = (c − a) ÷ (b + d); if b ÷ d > 1 cycles widen.

en.title: Commodity Markets, Boards and Exchanges
en.short: Organised markets, warehouse receipts, marketing boards, and hedging with futures and contract farming.

sections.heading: Organised markets and exchanges
sections.text:
An organised commodity market is a rule-governed place, physical or electronic, where a standardised commodity is traded. A commodity exchange runs it, setting grades and contract sizes, licensing members and publishing prices. Examples include the Ethiopia Commodity Exchange (2008), the Ghana Commodity Exchange and AFEX in Nigeria.

A warehouse receipt, issued by a licensed warehouse, confirms that a stated quantity and grade is stored. The holder can sell it or pledge it as loan collateral without moving the produce, so a farmer need not sell at harvest when prices are lowest.

sections.heading: Marketing boards
sections.text:
A marketing board is a government agency with monopsony (single-buyer) power over a named export crop, buying at a price it sets. Nigeria’s boards grew out of the West African Produce Control Board of the 1940s and became regional bodies in the 1950s, such as the Western Region cocoa board. They steadied prices and funded research, but often paid farmers below world prices and kept the surplus.

Nigeria wound its boards up in the mid-1980s under structural adjustment. Ghana still runs a cocoa board (COCOBOD).

sections.heading: Hedging and contracts
sections.text:
A forward contract is a private agreement to deliver a set quantity at a set price on a set date; each side bears default risk. A futures contract is the standardised, exchange-traded form, cleared with margins and daily settlement. Hedging means an offsetting futures position that cancels cash price risk.

A farmer will sell 10 tonnes of maize in three months. He sells a 10-tonne futures contract at ₦250,000 a tonne. At harvest spot is ₦210,000 and he buys back at ₦215,000.
Cash sale: 10 × 210,000 = ₦2,100,000.
Futures gain: 10 × (250,000 − 215,000) = ₦350,000.
Total ₦2,450,000, or ₦245,000 a tonne. The basis is spot minus futures: 210,000 − 215,000 = −₦5,000, which is why the effective price is ₦5,000 below the opening futures price. This basis risk is what hedging cannot remove.

Contract farming is an agreement in which a buyer supplies inputs or credit and the farmer delivers agreed quantity and quality at an agreed price.

keyPoints: A commodity exchange sets grades and contract sizes, licenses members and publishes prices.
A warehouse receipt proves stored quantity and grade and can be sold or pledged as collateral.
Marketing boards bought export crops at set prices; they steadied prices but taxed farmers through low prices.
A forward contract is private and carries default risk; a futures contract is standardised and cleared.
Hedging locks in a price: effective price = spot at sale + gain or loss on futures = opening futures price + basis.
Contract farming shifts price and market risk to the buyer but can create dependence and side-selling.

en.title: Agricultural Cooperatives and Rural Institutions
en.short: Principles, types and structure of agricultural cooperatives, rural institutions and their management problems.

sections.heading: Principles and identity
sections.text: A cooperative is a member-owned business controlled democratically, run to serve members rather than outside investors. The International Cooperative Alliance’s Statement on Cooperative Identity (1995) lists seven principles: voluntary and open membership; democratic member control; member economic participation; autonomy and independence; education, training and information; cooperation among cooperatives; and concern for community. In a primary agricultural society, each member normally has one vote, regardless of shares. Surplus may be shared as a patronage refund, in proportion to use. These principles are international, but national cooperative law and registration differ by country.

sections.heading: Types and structure
sections.text: Common types are thrift and credit societies, where members save and borrow from a common fund; marketing cooperatives, which pool produce to sell and bargain better; and multipurpose societies, which combine credit, input supply and marketing. Producer groups and farmers associations may be looser bodies that share information, train members and represent farmers, but they are not always registered cooperatives. Rural institutions are the organisations and rules that shape rural economic life; cooperatives are one type. Structure often runs from primary societies to secondary unions or federations to a national apex, but names and legal forms vary by country.

sections.heading: Case and management problems
sections.text: Example: 40 members save 5,000 each monthly. Pool = 40 × 5,000 = 200,000. If 100,000 is lent for six months at a flat 2% per month, interest = 100,000 × 0.02 × 6 = 12,000. The fund must also cover defaults and running costs. Common problems include weak records, low capital, poor loan recovery, elite capture (leaders use the society for themselves), free-riding (members benefit without contributing), low participation, and unclear roles between committee and manager. Regular audits, written rules, member education and transparent meetings reduce these risks.

keyPoints: A cooperative is member-owned and democratically controlled, with one member one vote in primary societies.
The ICA’s seven principles cover open membership, democratic control, member economic participation, autonomy, education, cooperation among cooperatives and concern for community.
Thrift and credit, marketing and multipurpose societies are common agricultural types; producer groups and farmers associations may not be registered cooperatives.
Structure often runs from primary society to union or federation to apex, but legal forms vary by country.
Management problems include weak records, low capital, poor loan recovery, elite capture and low participation.
Transparent rules, audits, member education and active meetings strengthen governance.

en.title: Agricultural Policy, Planning and Programmes
en.short: Policy process, instruments, Nigerian and African plans, and monitoring and evaluation.

sections.heading: Policy and process
sections.text:
Agricultural policy is the set of deliberate government decisions that shape farming, food and rural livelihoods: what is produced, who is supported, and at what price. Markets alone can leave hunger and low farm incomes.

The policy process runs through agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation, which feeds back into the next round. In practice the stages overlap.

Common objectives are food security, farm incomes, price stability, rural employment and sustainability. They conflict: cheap food helps consumers but lowers farm prices.

sections.heading: Instruments
sections.text:
Instruments are the tools. A tariff is a tax on imports; it raises the domestic price, protecting producers but costing consumers. A subsidy lowers a cost or raises a return. Input programmes supply seed, fertiliser or credit. Research funding pays for breeding, agronomy and extension; returns are slow but large.

Example: a 50 kg bag of fertiliser costs 30,000 naira. A 50 per cent subsidy leaves the farmer paying 15,000 naira and government paying 15,000 naira. For 100,000 bags: 15,000 × 100,000 = 1.5 billion naira. Worth it only if the extra yield covers that cost.

sections.heading: Plans in Africa
sections.text:
Nigeria has run Operation Feed the Nation (1976), the Green Revolution (1980), the National Agricultural Policy (1988), the Agricultural Transformation Agenda (2011-2015), the Agricultural Promotion Policy (2016-2020) and the National Agricultural Technology and Innovation Policy (NATIP, 2022-2027). The Agricultural Development Programmes, begun in 1975 with World Bank support, set the area-based project model.

Across Africa, the Comprehensive Africa Agriculture Development Programme (CAADP) was adopted in 2003, with a pledge of 10 per cent of national budgets to agriculture; the Malabo Declaration of 2014 renewed it. Ethiopia’s Agricultural Development Led Industrialization (ADLI) and Kenya’s Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy (ASTGS) are national examples. Targets change; check official sources.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
sections.text: Monitoring is continuous: it tracks inputs, activities and outputs against the plan. Evaluation is periodic and asks whether outcomes changed and whether the programme caused it. Evaluation needs a baseline, a comparison group and a theory of change; without them a yield rise cannot be credited to the policy.

keyPoints: Agricultural policy is deliberate government action on farming, food and rural livelihoods, used where markets alone leave hunger or low incomes.
The policy process is agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation, which feeds back into the next round.
Objectives conflict, so policy always involves trade-offs between cheap food, farm incomes and sustainability.
A tariff protects producers and costs consumers; a subsidy or input programme lowers costs but needs budget and targeting checks.
Nigeria moved from Operation Feed the Nation (1976) to APP (2016-2020) and NATIP (2022-2027); CAADP (2003) set a continental 10 per cent budget pledge, renewed at Malabo in 2014.
Monitoring tracks inputs and outputs continuously; evaluation asks whether outcomes changed and needs a baseline and a comparison group.

en.title: Agricultural Project Analysis and Appraisal
en.short: Projects, the project cycle, cost-benefit analysis, discounting, NPV, BCR and sensitivity testing.

sections.heading: Projects and the cycle
sections.text:
A project is a set of coordinated activities with a defined objective, location, budget and time limit, such as a small irrigation scheme. The project cycle usually runs: identification; preparation or feasibility study; appraisal; implementation with monitoring; and evaluation.

Identification screens ideas. Preparation designs the project and tests technical, financial, economic, social and environmental feasibility. Appraisal is an independent ex ante review before funding. Implementation carries out and monitors work. Evaluation compares results with targets after completion.

sections.heading: Discounting and decision rules
sections.text:
Cost-benefit analysis compares a project’s incremental benefits and costs over its life. Financial analysis uses market cash flows; economic analysis values gains and losses to society, often with shadow prices. Because money later is worth less, discount each year’s net flow: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^t, where r is the discount rate and t the year.

NPV = Σ(Bt − Ct) ÷ (1 + r)^t. BCR = PV of benefits ÷ PV of costs. Accept an independent project if NPV > 0 or BCR > 1; among mutually exclusive projects, choose the highest NPV.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
An agro-processing project costs 100,000 now and earns net benefits of 60,000 in year 1 and 60,000 in year 2. At r = 10%, PV year 1 = 60,000 ÷ 1.10 = 54,545.45; PV year 2 = 60,000 ÷ 1.21 = 49,586.78. Total PV benefits = 104,132.23.

NPV = 104,132.23 − 100,000 = 4,132.23. BCR = 104,132.23 ÷ 100,000 = 1.04. The project passes, but the margin is thin; a 10% fall in benefits makes NPV negative.

sections.heading: Sensitivity and pitfalls
sections.text:
Sensitivity analysis recalculates NPV or BCR under changed assumptions, such as lower yields or delayed benefits.

Pitfalls include optimistic forecasts, double counting, ignoring working capital, mixing nominal cash flows with a real discount rate, and omitting residual or environmental costs. Include all incremental cash flows and state the discount rate and its source.

keyPoints: A project has a defined objective, location, budget and time limit; the cycle runs identification, preparation, appraisal, implementation and evaluation.
Discounting converts future cash flows to present value: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^t.
NPV = Σ(Bt − Ct) ÷ (1 + r)^t; accept an independent project when NPV > 0.
BCR = PV of benefits ÷ PV of costs; accept when BCR > 1, but use NPV to rank mutually exclusive projects.
Sensitivity analysis tests NPV or BCR under changed yields, costs, prices or delays.
Common pitfalls are optimistic forecasts, double counting, omitted working capital and inconsistent price or discount assumptions.

en.title: Agricultural Trade and Commodity Development
en.short: Comparative advantage, tariffs, quotas, standards and commodity programmes for cocoa, oil palm, cassava and shea.

sections.heading: Trade and advantage
sections.text:
Agricultural trade is cross-border buying and selling of farm commodities. A country exports goods it can produce at lower opportunity cost and imports others. Comparative advantage is producing a good at lower opportunity cost than a trading partner, even if the partner is more efficient at everything. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best use of resources.

Example: Country A needs 100 labour hours for 1 tonne cocoa or 50 for cassava. Country B needs 200 for cocoa and 50 for cassava. A’s opportunity cost of 1 cocoa is 2 cassava; B’s is 4. A has comparative advantage in cocoa, B in cassava. If A trades 1 cocoa for 3 cassava, A gains 1 cassava over its own cost, and B pays 3 instead of 4. Both gain.

sections.heading: Trade measures
sections.text: Tariffs are taxes on imports. Quotas limit imported quantity. Subsidies lower producers’ costs or raise export competitiveness. Licences, export bans, sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) rules and technical standards also control trade. SPS measures protect health; technical barriers cover labelling and quality. The WTO Agreement on Agriculture disciplines market access, domestic support and export subsidies, while the SPS and TBT Agreements set rules for food safety and standards. Effects on farmers are mixed. Protection can raise local prices and incomes, but tariffs on inputs raise costs. Strict standards open high-value markets but require costly compliance. Export bans can depress farm-gate prices.

sections.heading: Procedures and programmes
sections.text: Exporters usually register, obtain licences, arrange inspection, phytosanitary and quality certificates, customs clearance and payment documents; importers follow the destination country’s rules. Quality standards cover moisture, defects, contamination and traceability, and vary by buyer and country, so check current official requirements. Commodity development programmes support productivity, grading, processing and market access. Examples include cocoa rehabilitation, oil palm expansion, cassava processing and shea butter quality projects, often with cooperatives and women’s groups.

keyPoints: Comparative advantage compares opportunity costs, not absolute productivity.
Opportunity cost of cocoa = labour hours per tonne cocoa ÷ labour hours per tonne cassava.
Tariffs tax imports; quotas limit import quantity; SPS and technical standards regulate safety and quality.
Trade rules can raise farm prices but also raise input costs and compliance costs.
Export procedures usually include registration, licences, inspection, phytosanitary and quality certificates, customs and payment documents.
