Commodity programmes aim to improve productivity, quality, processing and market access for crops such as cocoa, oil palm, cassava and shea.

en.title: Food Economics, Nutrition and Food Security
en.short: Food security pillars, food demand and Engel’s law, balance sheets, food aid and hunger measures.

sections.heading: Food security defined
sections.text:
Food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical, social and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that meets dietary needs and food preferences for an active, healthy life. Its four pillars are availability (enough food), access (households can obtain it), utilisation (safe food, clean water and health care), and stability (the pillars hold through shocks).

Food insecurity may be chronic or transitory.

sections.heading: Food demand and Engel’s law
sections.text:
Food demand is the quantity households buy at given prices and incomes. Income elasticity is the percentage change in quantity or spending divided by the percentage change in income. Engel’s law says the share of income spent on food falls as income rises, though absolute spending may rise.

Example: income rises from 50,000 to 60,000 and food spending from 25,000 to 27,000. The food share falls from 50% to 45%. Expenditure elasticity is (2,000 ÷ 25,000) ÷ (10,000 ÷ 50,000) = 0.4.

sections.heading: Balance sheets and food aid
sections.text:
A food balance sheet is a national account of food supply and use for a period. Supply includes production, imports and opening stocks. Use includes food, feed, seed, waste, exports and closing stocks. Food supply divided by population gives apparent per capita availability, in kilocalories per day. It is not actual intake.

Food aid is food, or money to buy food, given to people in need. It can be in-kind, cash-based or locally purchased. It helps emergencies but must be needs-based and must not depress local production or markets.

sections.heading: Hunger measures and Africa
sections.text:
Hunger is measured differently. The prevalence of undernourishment estimates the share of people whose dietary energy is below requirements. The Food Insecurity Experience Scale asks about worry, skipped meals and running out of food. Anthropometry measures stunting (low height-for-age), wasting (low weight-for-height) and underweight (low weight-for-age). Each answers a different question.

In Nigeria and Africa, conflict, climate shocks, poverty and food price inflation are major drivers. Figures differ by survey and year; check the latest FAO, WFP, UNICEF and national statistics reports.

keyPoints: Food security rests on availability, access, utilisation and stability.
Engel’s law: food’s share of household income falls as income rises.
Food expenditure elasticity = percentage change in food spending ÷ percentage change in income.
A food balance sheet estimates apparent per capita food availability, not actual intake.
Food aid should be needs-based and should not undermine local production or markets.
Hunger measures include prevalence of undernourishment, FIES and anthropometry; check current country data.

en.title: Agribusiness Management and Agricultural Value Chains
en.short: Agribusiness planning and budgeting, value chain mapping, upgrading and margins.

sections.heading: Agribusiness and firms
sections.text: Agribusiness means all the firms and activities that supply farms, produce on farms, process, distribute and retail food and fibre. It includes input suppliers, farmers, agro-processors, transporters, wholesalers and retailers. Each type has a different business plan. An input supplier needs stock, credit and storage plans; a farm needs production and cash-flow plans; a processor needs capacity and quality plans; a retailer needs sales and wastage plans. Management means planning, organising, directing and controlling these resources. A business plan states the goal, market, operations, costs, expected returns and risks. It is a guide, not a guarantee.

sections.heading: Budgets and margins
sections.text: An enterprise budget lists expected receipts and costs for one activity. Variable costs change with output; fixed costs do not. Gross margin equals gross receipts minus variable costs. It helps compare enterprises when fixed costs are shared. A cash-flow budget shows when money enters and leaves, which matters because farming is seasonal. Worked example: a fertiliser retailer buys 100 bags at 20,000 each (2,000,000), pays 50,000 handling, and sells all at 23,000 each (2,300,000). Gross margin = 2,300,000 − 2,000,000 − 50,000 = 250,000. Fixed costs of 100,000 give profit 150,000. Include stock, credit and spoilage.

sections.heading: Value chains and mapping
sections.text: A value chain is the sequence of actors and activities that add value as a product moves from input supply to the final buyer. Chain mapping draws actors, product, money and information flows and marks bottlenecks such as poor roads, weak storage or delayed payment. Upgrading means improving products, processes, functions or channels to capture more value. The market margin is the final price minus the farm price; the farmer’s share is farm price divided by final price. If the farm price is 300 and the retail price 500, the margin is 200 and the farmer’s share is 300 ÷ 500 = 60%. Links between farmers, processors and buyers range from spot markets (one-off sales at the going price) to contracts and cooperatives. Strong links need trust, grades, reliable delivery and fair risk sharing.

keyPoints: Agribusiness covers input supply, farming, processing, distribution and retail.
An enterprise budget lists all expected receipts and costs for one activity; gross margin = gross receipts − variable costs.
A cash-flow budget tracks the timing of money, not only the total.
Chain mapping shows actors, flows and bottlenecks in a value chain.
Market margin = final price − farm price; farmer’s share = farm price ÷ final price × 100.
Upgrading and fair links help farmers and processors capture more value.

en.title: Agricultural Extension and Technology Adoption
en.short: Extension methods, adoption and diffusion of farm innovations, and planning and evaluation.

sections.heading: Extension systems
sections.text: Extension is education and advice linking research with farmers. Public services are run by government. Private advisory services are sold by agribusinesses, input dealers or consultants, and cooperatives or NGOs also advise. Methods include farm visits, group meetings, demonstrations and radio. Training and visit (T&V) used regular visits by village extension workers to contact farmers, with close supervision. The World Bank promoted it in the 1970s and 1980s, but it was costly and could favour better-off farmers. Farmer field schools are season-long group learning, often for integrated pest management: farmers observe, experiment and discuss in their fields. Private advice can be efficient but may exclude poor farmers or push purchased inputs.

sections.heading: Adoption and diffusion
sections.text: Adoption is a farmer’s decision to use an innovation; diffusion is its spread through a farming community over time. Rogers describes innovators, early adopters, the early majority, late majority and laggards. Uptake depends on the innovation’s relative advantage, compatibility with the farm and culture, complexity, trialability and observability. It also depends on risk, capital, labour, land, market access, information and tenure. For example, Amina, a smallholder in Kano State, Nigeria, sees a neighbour’s higher maize yield. She tries the seed on a small plot because the gain is visible and the trial is cheap. A credit constraint may still stop her scaling up.

sections.heading: Planning and evaluation
sections.text: Extension planning starts with a needs assessment and clear objectives for a named target group. Planners choose methods, staff, budget and a calendar. Supervision supports field staff and checks that visits and demonstrations happen. Monitoring tracks activities and outputs, such as farmers reached. Evaluation compares outcomes or impact with a baseline, using indicators such as adoption rates or yields. Good evaluation asks whether change came from the extension programme, not from weather or prices.

keyPoints: Extension links research and farmers through public, private, cooperative and NGO services.
Training and visit used regular supervised visits to contact farmers but was costly and could favour better-off farmers.
Farmer field schools are season-long, field-based group learning, often used in integrated pest management.
Adoption is the decision to use an innovation; diffusion is its spread through a community.
Relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability affect uptake, along with risk, capital and market access.
Plan extension from needs and objectives, supervise staff, monitor activities and evaluate outcomes against a baseline.

en.title: Natural Resource and Environmental Economics in Agriculture
en.short: Applying economics to farm land, water, forests, fisheries, wildlife, externalities, valuation and climate.

sections.heading: Externalities and rights
sections.text: An externality is a cost or benefit from a farm decision that falls on others and is not in the market price. Pesticide drift, fertiliser runoff and eroded soil silting a river are negative externalities. Tree cover, hedges and wetlands that store water can give positive ones. Taxes, subsidies, regulation or payments for ecosystem services can correct them. Property rights matter: common property has a defined user group and rules; open access has no effective exclusion.

sections.heading: Common pool resources
sections.text: Common pool resources are rival in use but hard to exclude people from: grazing land, irrigation water, forests, fisheries and wildlife. Under open access each user takes the gain and shares the loss, so use exceeds the sustainable level and rent is dissipated. Remedies include licences, quotas, closed seasons, community rules and co-management. Common property is not doomed; rules work when boundaries, monitoring and sanctions are clear.

sections.heading: Valuing and conservation
sections.text: Environmental goods lack market prices. Revealed-preference methods infer value from behaviour: market price, replacement cost, travel cost and hedonic pricing (land values). Stated-preference methods ask: contingent valuation and choice experiments. Cost-benefit analysis compares discounted benefits and costs using NPV = Σ (Bt − Ct) ÷ (1 + r)^t. Example: a farmer spends 120,000 now on erosion control and gains 30,000 at the end of each of five years. At r = 10%, the annuity factor is 3.7908, so PV benefits = 30,000 × 3.7908 = 113,724. NPV = 113,724 − 120,000 = −6,276, so reject. At r = 5%, PV = 129,884 and NPV = +9,884, so accept. Discount rate matters.

sections.heading: Climate and land use
sections.text: Climate change affects agriculture through heat, drought, floods and pests. Adaptation includes drought-tolerant varieties, irrigation, changed planting dates and insurance. Mitigation includes storing carbon in soil and trees, reduced tillage and agroforestry. Sustainable land use weighs private profit against soil loss, water use, biodiversity and yields. Carbon taxes, cap-and-trade, subsidies, secure tenure and extension can change incentives, but uncertainty and long time horizons make decisions hard.

keyPoints: An externality is a cost or benefit not reflected in market prices; taxes, subsidies, regulation or payments can internalise it.
Open access causes overuse; common property can be sustainable when users, boundaries, monitoring and sanctions are clear.
Revealed-preference methods use observed behaviour; stated-preference methods ask people about hypothetical choices.
NPV = Σ (Bt − Ct) ÷ (1 + r)^t; accept a conservation project when NPV is positive.
A higher discount rate lowers the present value of future benefits and can reverse a conservation decision.
Climate policy combines adaptation, mitigation and secure land tenure, but long horizons and uncertainty complicate choices.

en.title: Farm Management Research and the Field Study
en.short: Methods of farm management research, survey design, sampling, fieldwork, data quality and report writing.

sections.heading: Research types
sections.text: Farm management research studies farm decisions: what to produce, how, and with what resources. Common types are the diagnostic survey, which describes current practice and problems; the case study, which examines one farm in depth; and model based studies, which compare plans using budgets or programming. Methods include farm records, structured surveys, interviews, observation and field experiments. Choose the method that fits the question and state its limits.

sections.heading: Survey and sampling
sections.text: Survey design starts with clear objectives and a defined population, the whole group studied. A sampling frame is the list from which the sample is drawn. Probability sampling gives every listed unit a known chance of selection: simple random, stratified and cluster sampling are common. Non-probability methods such as purposive or convenience sampling are useful for exploration but do not support generalisation. Sample size depends on the aim, variability and resources; check your department’s guide. For example, a student studying 120 poultry farmers in one district may draw 30 by simple random sampling from a complete list and interview them with a pre-tested schedule.

sections.heading: Questionnaire and fieldwork
sections.text: A questionnaire should be short, clear and in the respondent’s language. Use closed questions for easy coding and open questions for explanation. Avoid leading, double-barrelled and ambiguous items. Pre-test with a few farmers and revise. Interviewing requires consent, privacy, neutral tone and consistent order. Record answers at the time. Data quality control includes training enumerators, a pilot test, daily checks for missing or impossible values, back-checks on a sample, and careful cleaning before analysis.

sections.heading: Report and referencing
sections.text: A field study or farm practice report usually has preliminary pages, introduction and problem statement, objectives, literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and recommendations, references and appendices. Link each result to an objective, use tables and figures clearly, and avoid unsupported claims. Referencing must follow your department’s required style, such as APA or another named style, and be consistent. Programmes differ by country and institution, so check the current departmental guide.

keyPoints: Farm management research may be diagnostic, case study or model based; choose the method to fit the question.
A sample can be generalised only if drawn by probability methods from a defined sampling frame.
Questionnaire items must be clear, pre-tested, and free of leading or double-barrelled wording.
Interviewing requires consent, neutral conduct and recording answers at the time.
Data quality control includes training, pilot testing, daily checks, back-checks and cleaning.
Field study reports follow a standard structure and a consistent referencing style required by the department.

en.title: Professional Ethics and Practice in Agricultural Economics
en.short: Duties to clients, farmers, employers and public, data honesty, conflict disclosure, professional bodies and fieldwork.

sections.heading: Duties and trust
sections.text: Professional ethics are the standards of conduct expected of someone who uses specialist knowledge to serve others. An agricultural economist owes duties to clients who pay for analysis, to farmers and rural people affected by advice, to employers, and to the public. The core duties are competence, honesty, confidentiality and care. Advice to farmers should be in plain language, with costs, risks and alternatives stated. Do not exploit a farmer’s weaker bargaining position or raise false hopes about yields or prices. Duty to an employer does not justify hiding bad results or breaking the law.

sections.heading: Data and disclosure
sections.text: Honesty in data means no fabrication, no falsification and no selective reporting. Fabrication means inventing data; falsification means altering it. Keep raw records, describe methods, report limitations and correct errors openly. A conflict of interest exists when a personal interest could bias professional judgement. Disclose fees, commissions, funding, ownership or family links before advising. Responsible advice stays within your competence, separates facts from assumptions, gives a range where evidence is uncertain, and refers difficult legal, veterinary or financial matters to qualified people. Never guarantee a profit.

sections.heading: Bodies and fieldwork
sections.text: The Farm Management Association of Nigeria (FMAN) is a Nigerian professional body for farm management specialists. The International Farm Management Association (IFMA) is an international body linking farm management professionals. They support training, conferences and professional exchange; check their current codes and membership rules rather than assuming one global code. In consultancy, agree written terms of reference (scope, timing and fee), confidentiality and deliverables. In fieldwork, obtain permission and informed consent, meaning people understand the purpose and risks before agreeing. Protect privacy, pay fairly, respect local customs and avoid harm.

sections.heading: Short case
sections.text: A Nigerian adviser is paid by a fertiliser supplier to evaluate a product. She discloses the payment, uses independent trial plots, reports the yield gain with a confidence range, and notes that results vary by soil. The client can then judge the advice fairly.

keyPoints: Professional ethics require competence, honesty, confidentiality and care towards clients, farmers, employers and the public.
Never fabricate, falsify or selectively report data; keep raw records and state limitations.
Disclose any conflict of interest, such as fees, funding or ownership, before giving advice.
Give responsible advice within your competence, state assumptions and uncertainty, and refer matters you are not qualified to handle.
FMAN is a Nigerian farm management body and IFMA is an international one; check their current codes and membership rules.
In consultancy use written terms of reference; in fieldwork obtain permission and informed consent, protect privacy and avoid harm.

en.title: Advanced Production Economics and Farm Firm Theory
en.short: Covers duality, profit, cost and distance functions, productivity indices, frontiers and farm risk.

sections.heading: Duality and functions
sections.text:
Duality means a technology can be described by maximising profit or minimising cost. The profit function π(p,w) is maximum profit at output price p and input price w. The cost function C(w,y) is least cost of output y.

Hotelling’s lemma gives supply ∂π/∂p = y and input demand ∂π/∂w = −x; Shephard’s lemma gives ∂C/∂w = x. An output distance function D(x,y) measures distance from the frontier: D = 1 on it, D < 1 inside. It suits missing prices or multiple outputs.

sections.heading: Worked duality example
sections.text:
Example: y = √x, so x = y² and C(w,y) = w y². Profit π = p y − w y².

Setting p − 2w y = 0 gives y* = p ÷ (2w). If p = 20 and w = 5, y* = 2, x* = 4, π = 40 − 20 = 20. The profit function is π(p,w) = p² ÷ (4w) = 400 ÷ 20 = 20.

sections.heading: Productivity and frontiers
sections.text:
Technical change shifts the frontier; productivity compares output with all inputs. Total factor productivity (TFP) is often measured by a Tornqvist index: ln(TFP_t ÷ TFP_0) = Σ_i 0.5(s_i,t + s_i,0) ln(y_i,t ÷ y_i,0) − Σ_j 0.5(s_j,t + s_j,0) ln(x_j,t ÷ x_j,0), where s_i are revenue shares and s_j are cost shares.

Frontier methods estimate best practice. Data envelopment analysis (DEA) is nonparametric; stochastic frontier analysis (SFA) separates inefficiency from noise. The Malmquist index splits TFP change into technical change and efficiency change.

sections.heading: Household and risk
sections.text:
The farm household model treats production and consumption jointly: the household maximises utility over goods and leisure subject to a budget that includes farm profit. With complete markets, the production and consumption choices separate; when a market such as labour is missing, a shadow wage replaces the market wage and the choices must be solved jointly.

A multiproduct firm chooses output mix under risk; expected utility or mean-variance criteria replace simple profit maximisation. Covariance between enterprise returns matters, so diversification can reduce risk. Constraints include land, labour, credit and information.

keyPoints: Duality links the profit function π(p,w), the cost function C(w,y) and the output distance function D(x,y).
Hotelling’s lemma: ∂π/∂p = y and ∂π/∂w = −x; Shephard’s lemma: ∂C/∂w = x.
The output distance function equals 1 on the frontier and is below 1 for an inefficient output bundle.
The Tornqvist TFP index is ln(TFP_t ÷ TFP_0) = Σ_i 0.5(s_i,t + s_i,0) ln(y_i,t ÷ y_i,0) − Σ_j 0.5(s_j,t + s_j,0) ln(x_j,t ÷ x_j,0), with s_i revenue shares and s_j cost shares.
DEA and SFA estimate production frontiers, and the Malmquist index separates technical change from efficiency change.
Farm households jointly choose production and consumption, while multiproduct firms under risk use expected utility or mean-variance criteria.

en.title: Econometrics for Agricultural and Food Data
en.short: Regression, panel and limited dependent models for farm and food data, with endogeneity and impact evaluation.

sections.heading: Regression and panels
sections.text:
Multiple regression estimates how several farm or household traits move an outcome together: y = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + u. Each coefficient is a partial effect, holding other regressors fixed. Panel data follow the same farms over time. A fixed effects model, y_it = α_i + βx_it + u_it, removes each farm’s time-invariant traits, such as soil type, so β comes from within-farm change. Random effects assumes those traits are uncorrelated with x; a Hausman test helps choose.

Heteroskedasticity means error variance changes with regressors; autocorrelation means errors are correlated over time. Both make usual standard errors wrong. Use robust or cluster-robust standard errors, clustered by farm or village.

sections.heading: Limited outcomes and selection
sections.text:
Limited dependent variable models handle outcomes that are not continuous. A binary adoption outcome, y = 1 if a farmer adopts, is modelled by logit: P(y = 1) = 1 ÷ (1 + e^−(β0 + β1x)). Coefficients are effects on log odds (the log of the odds of adopting); report marginal effects. A censored outcome, such as pesticide spending with many zeros, suits Tobit. Counts, such as visits, suit Poisson or negative binomial regression.

Endogeneity means a regressor is correlated with the error, often through omitted variables, measurement error or reverse causality. Instrumental variables need an instrument that affects x but not y except through x. Sample selection arises when observed farms differ from the target population, for example only profitable farms keep records; Heckman-type models can correct it under strong assumptions.

sections.heading: Experiments and impact
sections.text:
Field experiments randomise a treatment, such as fertiliser subsidy or training, across farms. Design needs power, a credible control, and attention to attrition and spillovers. Impact evaluation estimates a counterfactual. Difference-in-differences compares change in treated and control groups.

Example: treated yields rise from 10 to 14 bags, control from 8 to 10. Effect = (14 − 10) − (10 − 8) = 2 bags. Randomisation makes groups comparable; DiD relies on a parallel trends assumption, meaning treated and control would have moved the same way without treatment. Report intention-to-treat effects (the effect of being offered the treatment, whether or not farms take it up) and check assumptions.

keyPoints: Multiple regression gives partial effects: y = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + u.
Fixed effects remove time-invariant farm traits: y_it = α_i + βx_it + u_it.
Logit models binary outcomes: P(y = 1) = 1 ÷ (1 + e^−(β0 + β1x)).
Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation make usual standard errors wrong; use robust or cluster-robust standard errors.
Endogeneity needs instrumental variables or other identification; sample selection needs Heckman-type correction under strong assumptions.
The difference-in-differences effect is (treated after − treated before) − (control after − control before).

en.title: Food Policy, Agricultural Transformation and Development
en.short: Agricultural transformation, agriculture in development, food policy, trade, volatility, social protection and the SDGs.

sections.heading: Growth and transformation
sections.text: Structural transformation is the long-run fall in agriculture’s shares of output and employment as incomes rise. Productivity must rise, or food shortages and poverty follow. Lewis’s dual-economy model explains labour moving from low-productivity farms to industry, but it assumes surplus labour and can neglect agricultural investment. Schultz argued that traditional farmers are poor but efficient; they respond to profitable technology and incentives. Induced innovation theory (Hayami and Ruttan) says relative factor prices steer research toward saving the scarce factor, such as labour-saving machinery where wages are high. Agriculture also supplies food, raw materials and foreign exchange. In a rice district, irrigation raises yields; higher incomes let households buy from local traders.

sections.heading: Policy design and trade
sections.text: Food policy sets objectives and chooses instruments: public investment, input subsidies, price supports, trade measures, regulation and social protection. Design must state the market failure and target group. Evaluation compares outcomes with a counterfactual, what would have happened without the policy. Randomised trials or quasi-experiments can estimate impacts; cost-effectiveness and distribution matter. Trade lets countries use comparative advantage, but tariffs and export bans change prices and can hurt poor net buyers (households that buy more food than they sell). Suppose a government wants to raise maize output. A fertiliser subsidy may raise yields but often favours larger farms; targeted extension plus a cash transfer may cost less per poor farmer. The choice depends on evidence, not ideology.

sections.heading: Volatility, protection, SDGs
sections.text: Food prices are volatile because supply depends on weather and pests, demand is inelastic, stocks are costly, and trade restrictions can amplify shocks. Volatility hurts poor net buyers. Responses include market information, strategic reserves, risk insurance, trade and social protection. Social protection includes cash transfers, food aid, school feeding and public works; transfers can protect consumption and relax credit constraints, helping farmers invest. Sustainable Development Goals frame policy: SDG 2 aims to end hunger and promote sustainable agriculture; SDG 1 targets poverty; SDG 13 climate action and SDG 15 life on land matter. Balance short-run relief with long-run productivity.

keyPoints: Structural transformation means agriculture’s shares of output and employment fall while productivity rises.
Schultz argued that traditional farmers are poor but efficient and respond to profitable technology and incentives.
Induced innovation directs research toward saving the scarcest factor.
Policy evaluation needs a credible counterfactual, not only before-and-after comparison.
Trade restrictions and thin stocks can amplify food price volatility, hurting poor net buyers.
Social protection and SDG 2 can protect consumption and support farm investment when well targeted.

en.title: Frontier Topics in Agricultural Economics
en.short: Current research frontiers and how to frame a dissertation proposal in agricultural economics.

sections.heading: Frontier research areas
sections.text: Climate-smart agriculture is an approach, not one technology: it seeks higher and more stable farm incomes, adaptation to climate change, and lower emissions where possible. Digital agriculture uses digital tools and data across the food chain; precision farming applies them to site-specific decisions, such as variable fertiliser rates. Researchers compare adoption, yields, costs and resilience, and they test for trade-offs. Evidence depends on context, so ask who benefits and whether gains persist.

sections.heading: Behaviour and bioeconomy
sections.text: Behavioural economics studies how psychology, norms and biases shape farm decisions. Experimental economics tests causes with controlled trials, often randomised field experiments. Random assignment creates a comparison group, but ethics and local consent are essential. Bioeconomy means economic activity based on renewable biological resources; circular systems keep residues and nutrients in use. A researcher must define the outcome and the counterfactual, meaning what would have happened without the intervention.

sections.heading: Gender and youth
sections.text: Gender analysis asks how roles, rights and access to land, credit, information and markets differ between women and men, and how projects affect each. Youth research examines entry into farming, skills, finance and employment. Use sex-disaggregated data, separated by sex, and ask who controls income and decisions. Avoid treating women or youth as one group; measure intra-household differences and report limitations.

sections.heading: Reading and proposing
sections.text: Read papers by mapping question, theory, data, identification strategy (how the study isolates cause) and limits. Use systematic reviews and recent journal articles, and check whether the method suits the question. A proposal states a problem, a specific gap, research questions, framework, data and method, ethics, timeline and contribution. Write it around one answerable question, not a broad topic. Case: a student in Kano plans a field experiment on SMS weather alerts and fertiliser use among maize farmers. She defines treatment, control, outcome, sample size and consent before collecting data.

keyPoints: Climate-smart agriculture pursues productivity, resilience and lower emissions together; it is not a single practice.
Digital agriculture uses data and digital tools; precision farming applies them to site-specific management.
Behavioural economics studies norms and biases; experimental economics uses controlled trials to test causes.
Bioeconomy uses renewable biological resources; circular systems reduce waste and reuse residues.
Gender and youth research needs disaggregated data and attention to intra-household differences.
A dissertation proposal needs a clear gap, answerable question, suitable method, ethics and feasible data plan.
